subject: mathematics
title: Cambridge Primary Mathematics Stage 5
audience: Cambridge Primary Stage 5 learners, about ages 9 to 10

sources.title: Cambridge Primary Mathematics 0096 Curriculum Framework
sources.note: Objective codes and wording follow framework version 1.1 (September 2020). Verify against a licensed centre copy of the framework before publishing.

units.strand: Number — place value, ordering and rounding
units.title: Place value, ordering and rounding

topics.title: Digit value in decimals
topics.summary: Extend place value beyond whole numbers into tenths and hundredths so learners can say what each decimal digit is worth.

objectives.text: Understand and explain the value of each digit in decimals (tenths and hundredths).

topics.scope: Decimals with tenths and hundredths only. Connect the place-value chart to the hundred-square grid. Use one worked decimal such as 3.47 and a different practice number.
restrictions: No thousandths or further decimal places.
No decimal addition or subtraction algorithms.

topics.title: Multiplying and dividing whole numbers by 10, 100 and 1000
topics.summary: Show how digits shift places when whole numbers are multiplied or divided by powers of ten — the digits move, a decimal point never does.

objectives.text: Use knowledge of place value to multiply and divide whole numbers by 10, 100 and 1000.

topics.scope: Whole numbers times or divided by 10, 100 and 1000 only. Correct the 'add a zero' misconception explicitly by showing digits shifting columns on the place-value chart.
restrictions: No decimals in this topic — that is the next lesson.

topics.title: Multiplying and dividing decimals by 10 and 100
topics.summary: Apply the same digit-shift rule to decimals so learners see tenths become ones and hundredths become tenths.

objectives.text: Use knowledge of place value to multiply and divide decimals by 10 and 100.

topics.scope: Decimals with up to two decimal places multiplied or divided by 10 and 100. Explicitly link back to whole-number shifts.

topics.title: Composing, decomposing and regrouping numbers
topics.summary: Build numbers from their place-value parts and break them apart again, including decimals, to prepare for flexible calculation.

objectives.text: Compose, decompose and regroup numbers, including decimals (tenths and hundredths).

topics.scope: Whole numbers to 999 999 and decimals to hundredths. Show regrouping such as 4.7 = 4 + 0.7 = 3 + 1.7 and non-standard partitions.
restrictions: Do not teach column addition with carrying — regrouping concept only.

topics.title: Rounding to the nearest whole number
topics.summary: Use a number line to decide which whole number a one-decimal-place number is closest to, including the halfway case.

objectives.text: Round numbers with one decimal place to the nearest whole number.

topics.scope: One decimal place to nearest whole number only. Cover the 5-tenths rounds-up convention on the number line.
restrictions: No rounding to tenths or hundredths.

topics.title: Counting in steps, including past zero
topics.summary: Count on and back in equal steps along a number line, extending beyond zero into negative numbers.

objectives.text: Count on and count back in steps of constant size, and extend beyond zero to include negative numbers.

topics.scope: Constant whole-number steps crossing zero. Use a number line with a marked step size; introduce negative numbers as positions, not as a new arithmetic.
restrictions: No fraction or decimal step sizes.

topics.title: Symbols for two unknown quantities
topics.summary: Use shapes or symbols to stand for two unknowns in addition and subtraction puzzles, and reason about what they could be.

objectives.text: Recognise the use of objects, shapes or symbols to represent two unknown quantities in addition and subtraction calculations.

topics.scope: Puzzles like triangle + square = 12 where the same symbol always means the same number. Bar models make the unknowns visible. Keep solutions to whole numbers.
restrictions: No algebraic letters or formal solving.

topics.title: Finding any term of a linear sequence
topics.summary: Turn repeated addition of a constant into multiplication so any term can be found without counting every step.

objectives.text: Use the relationship between repeated addition of a constant and multiplication to find any term of a linear sequence.

topics.scope: Linear sequences with a constant whole-number difference. Link term number times step plus start to the term value; keep first-term and step visible.
restrictions: No n-th term algebra notation like 3n + 2.

topics.title: Square and triangular number patterns
topics.summary: See square numbers as square arrays and triangular numbers as growing rows, and extend both patterns spatially.

objectives.text: Recognise and extend the spatial pattern of square and triangular numbers.

topics.scope: Squares to 10 by 10 and triangular numbers to 55 as spatial dot patterns. Emphasize the shape of each pattern, not formula memorisation.

topics.title: Adding and subtracting integers
topics.summary: Estimate then add and subtract integers including a negative, using the number line to make direction visible.

objectives.text: Estimate, add and subtract integers, including where one integer is negative.

topics.scope: Two-term additions and subtractions with one negative integer, e.g. 25 + (-10) and -15 + 30. Estimate first, then calculate.
restrictions: No subtracting a negative (no double negatives).
No multiplication or division of negatives.

topics.title: Laws of arithmetic that simplify calculations
topics.summary: Choose when reordering or regrouping makes a calculation easier — commutativity, associativity and friendly pairs.

objectives.text: Understand which law of arithmetic to apply to simplify calculations.

topics.scope: Choosing an easier order or grouping, e.g. 17 + 28 + 13 by pairing 17 and 13, or 5 times 14 times 2. Name the idea in words, not formal law names only.
restrictions: No algebraic proof of the laws.

topics.title: The order of operations
topics.summary: Discover why multiplication and division are done before addition and subtraction, using one clear worked example.

objectives.text: Understand that the four operations follow a particular order.

topics.scope: Expressions with two operations, e.g. 3 + 4 times 2. Show the wrong left-to-right answer as a misconception and correct it.
restrictions: No acronym drill without meaning — anchor in a story context.

topics.title: Multiplying numbers up to 1000
topics.summary: Estimate first, then multiply whole numbers up to 1000 by a one- or two-digit number using a written or area strategy.

objectives.text: Estimate and multiply whole numbers up to 1000 by 1-digit or 2-digit whole numbers.

topics.scope: Grid/area or short-multiplication layout for numbers like 243 times 6 or 45 times 23. Always estimate with a rounded value first.

topics.title: Dividing numbers up to 1000
topics.summary: Estimate then divide whole numbers up to 1000 by a one-digit number, interpreting any remainder sensibly.

objectives.text: Estimate and divide whole numbers up to 1000 by 1-digit whole numbers.

topics.scope: Short division with and without a remainder, e.g. 456 divided by 4 and 457 divided by 4. Discuss what the remainder means in a sharing context.

topics.title: Prime and composite numbers
topics.summary: Distinguish primes from composites by testing whether a number makes only one rectangle or several.

objectives.text: Understand and explain the difference between prime and composite numbers.

topics.scope: Numbers to 30. Use dot/area arrays: primes form only a single row, composites form other rectangles. 1 is neither.

topics.title: Divisibility tests for 4 and 8
topics.summary: Use factors and multiples to test whether numbers divide by 4 or 8 without doing the full division.

objectives.text: Use knowledge of factors and multiples to understand tests of divisibility by 4 and 8.

topics.scope: Last-two-digits test for 4 and halving-twice reasoning for 8 on numbers to 9999. Explain WHY the test works using place value.
restrictions: No tests for 3, 6, 9 or other numbers.
Keep it to understanding, not speed drills.

topics.title: Square numbers to 100
topics.summary: Recognise square numbers up to 100 as equal-sided arrays and connect them to multiplication.

objectives.text: Use knowledge of multiplication to recognise square numbers (from 1 to 100).

topics.scope: Squares 1, 4, 9 ... 100 as arrays and as n times n. Quick recognition, not memorised chanting.

units.strand: Number — fractions, decimals, percentages, ratio and proportion
units.title: Fractions and operators

topics.title: A fraction is a division
topics.summary: Understand three-quarters as three divided by four — the numerator shares into denominator parts.

objectives.text: Understand that a fraction can be represented as a division of the numerator by the denominator (unit fractions, three-quarters, tenths and hundredths).

topics.scope: Unit fractions, three-quarters, tenths and hundredths written as numerator divided by denominator. Use bar shading to show the sharing.
restrictions: No converting fractions to decimals by division yet.

topics.title: Fractions as operators
topics.summary: Apply a proper fraction to a quantity, like three-quarters of twenty, by dividing then multiplying the parts.

objectives.text: Understand that proper fractions can act as operators.

topics.scope: Proper fractions of whole-number quantities that divide evenly, e.g. three-quarters of 20. Bar model first: split the whole, then take parts.
restrictions: No answers that are fractions themselves.

topics.title: Improper fractions and mixed numbers
topics.summary: See that five-quarters and one-and-a-quarter name the same amount, and convert between the two forms.

objectives.text: Recognise that improper fractions and mixed numbers can have an equivalent value.

topics.scope: Convert between improper fractions and mixed numbers using bar pictures: count whole bars plus the leftover part.
restrictions: No simplifying fractions in this topic.

topics.title: Fractions, decimals and percentages that match
topics.summary: Recognise the same value wearing three costumes: a proper fraction, a one-decimal-place decimal and a percentage.

objectives.text: Recognise that proper fractions, decimals (one decimal place) and percentages can have equivalent values.

topics.scope: Tenths-family equivalents only: 1/2 = 0.5 = 50%, 1/4 = 0.25 = 25% (via fifty-hundredths), tenths such as 7/10 = 0.7 = 70%. Use the hundred square to prove equivalence.

topics.title: Adding and subtracting fractions
topics.summary: Estimate then add and subtract fractions whose denominators are equal or multiples of each other, converting with equivalent fractions.

objectives.text: Estimate, add and subtract fractions with the same denominator and denominators that are multiples of each other.

topics.scope: Same denominator first, then denominators that are multiples such as halves and quarters. Show the equivalent-fraction conversion on bars before the written step.
restrictions: No unrelated denominators like thirds plus fifths.
Keep answers proper or simple mixed numbers.

topics.title: Unit fractions times and divided by whole numbers
topics.summary: Estimate and compute a unit fraction multiplied by or divided by a whole number, anchored in bar pictures.

objectives.text: Estimate, multiply and divide unit fractions by a whole number.

topics.scope: Unit fractions only: 1/3 times 6 as 'three thirds', and 1/4 divided by 2 as sharing a quarter bar into two. Keep visuals exact.
restrictions: No non-unit fractions times whole numbers.
No dividing a whole by a fraction.

units.strand: Number — fractions, decimals, percentages, ratio and proportion
units.title: Decimals, percentages and ratio

topics.title: Percentages of shapes
topics.summary: Recognise percentages of shaded shapes and write a percentage as a fraction with denominator one hundred.

objectives.text: Recognise percentages of shapes, and write percentages as a fraction with denominator 100.

topics.scope: Hundred-square grids: shade cells, name the percent, write it as n over 100. Connect 50% to half a grid.
restrictions: No decimals here — equivalence is a later topic.

topics.title: Ordering decimals, fractions and percentages
topics.summary: Compare and order one-decimal-place numbers, same-denominator fractions and percentages using equals, greater and less symbols.

objectives.text: Understand the relative size of quantities to compare and order numbers with one decimal place, proper fractions with the same denominator and percentages, using the symbols =, > and <.

topics.scope: Mixed-format comparisons resolved by converting to one form, shown on a shared number line. Include deliberate equals cases like 0.5 and 50%.
restrictions: One decimal place; same-denominator fractions only.

topics.title: Adding and subtracting decimals
topics.summary: Estimate then add and subtract decimals with the same number of decimal places, keeping the decimal point columns aligned.

objectives.text: Estimate, add and subtract numbers with the same number of decimal places.

topics.scope: Tenths and hundredths with matching decimal places, e.g. 3.45 + 2.3 is NOT allowed (different places) — use 3.45 + 2.30 style pairs. Show place-value alignment, not just 'line up the dot'.
restrictions: Same number of decimal places only.
No carrying across more than two columns.

topics.title: Multiplying decimals by whole numbers
topics.summary: Estimate then multiply a one-decimal-place number by a one-digit whole number, using repeated addition or the shift-and-divide trick.

objectives.text: Estimate and multiply numbers with one decimal place by 1-digit whole numbers.

topics.scope: One decimal place times one digit, e.g. 2.4 times 3. Show both the repeated-addition view and the 'times ten, multiply, divide by ten' strategy.

topics.title: Ratio compares parts; proportion compares part to whole
topics.summary: Tell apart a ratio (part to part) from a proportion (part to whole) using one concrete shared context.

objectives.text: Understand that: a proportion compares part to whole; a ratio compares part to part of two or more quantities.

topics.scope: One context (e.g. coloured beads) described both ways: 3 red out of 8 total is a proportion; 3 red to 5 blue is a ratio. Bar model makes the parts visible.
restrictions: No ratio notation arithmetic or simplifying ratios.

topics.title: Time intervals smaller than one second
topics.summary: Meet tenths and hundredths of a second as real measurements in sport and timers.

objectives.text: Understand time intervals less than one second.

topics.scope: Tenths and hundredths of a second on stopwatch displays, e.g. sprint times. Connect to decimal place value; no physics units needed.
restrictions: No milliseconds conversion beyond display reading.

topics.title: Comparing times across time zones
topics.summary: Read analogue and digital 12- and 24-hour times and find what time it is in another place.

objectives.text: Compare times between time zones in digital notation (12- and 24-hour) and on analogue clocks.

topics.scope: Whole-hour time-zone offsets only, with analogue and digital reading side by side. e.g. London 14:00 while it is 19:30 somewhere is out — keep offsets to whole hours.

topics.title: Time intervals that bridge through 60
topics.summary: Find elapsed times in seconds, minutes and hours when the interval crosses an hour or minute boundary.

objectives.text: Find time intervals in seconds, minutes and hours that bridge through 60.

topics.scope: Counting on across a 60 boundary, e.g. 10:45 to 11:20. Use a number-line bridge strategy: to the next hour, then onward.
restrictions: No crossing more than one hour boundary.

topics.title: Time intervals as decimals and mixed units
topics.summary: Express the same interval as a decimal and in mixed units, like 1.5 hours and 1 hour 30 minutes.

objectives.text: Recognise that a time interval can be expressed as a decimal, or in mixed units.

topics.scope: Quarters and halves as decimals (0.25, 0.5, 0.75 hours) and mixed units. The key misconception: 1.5 hours is NOT 1 hour 50 minutes.

units.strand: Geometry and Measure — geometrical reasoning, shapes and measurements
units.title: Angles, shapes and symmetry

topics.title: Classifying triangles
topics.summary: Identify, describe, classify and sketch isosceles, equilateral and scalene triangles using angles and symmetry.

objectives.text: Identify, describe, classify and sketch isosceles, equilateral or scalene triangles, including reference to angles and symmetrical properties.

topics.scope: The three triangle types by side length, plus what that means for their angles and mirror symmetry.
restrictions: No angle-sum calculations (that is a separate topic).
No right-angled naming conventions beyond recognition.

topics.title: 3D shapes and cube nets
topics.summary: Describe and sketch 3D shapes in different orientations and test which arrangements of six squares fold into a cube.

objectives.text: Identify, describe and sketch 3D shapes in different orientations.
Identify and sketch different nets for a cube.

topics.scope: Cube, cuboid, prism and pyramid recognition in rotated orientations; cube nets checked by imagining the fold. Keep to faces/edges/vertices vocabulary.
restrictions: No nets for shapes other than the cube.

topics.title: Reflective symmetry
topics.summary: Use mirror lines to identify and complete symmetrical patterns on grids.

objectives.text: Use knowledge of reflective symmetry to identify and complete symmetrical patterns.

topics.scope: Vertical and horizontal mirror lines on square grids; complete the reflected half of a pattern. On a coordinate grid, reflected points keep the same distance from the mirror.

topics.title: Acute, right, obtuse and reflex angles
topics.summary: Estimate, compare and classify angles using the four geometric names.

objectives.text: Estimate, compare and classify angles, using geometric vocabulary including acute, right, obtuse and reflex.

topics.scope: The four angle types with a right angle as the benchmark. Estimate then classify drawn angles; reflex means more than a straight line.
restrictions: No protractor measurement to the degree — classification ranges are enough.

topics.title: Angles on a straight line sum to 180 degrees
topics.summary: Use the straight-line angle sum to calculate a missing angle.

objectives.text: Know that the sum of the angles on a straight line is 180°, and use this to calculate missing angles on a straight line.

topics.scope: Two or three angles sharing a straight line; missing angle by subtraction from 180.
restrictions: No angles around a point (360) in this topic.

units.strand: Geometry and Measure — geometrical reasoning, shapes and measurements
units.title: Perimeter and area

topics.title: Same perimeter, different area
topics.summary: Estimate and measure perimeter and area of 2D shapes and discover that fixing one does not fix the other.

objectives.text: Estimate and measure perimeter and area of 2D shapes, understanding that shapes with the same perimeter can have different areas and vice versa.

topics.scope: Rectangles on grid paper: 16-perimeter shapes with different areas, and same-area shapes with different perimeters. Count squares and boundary lengths.
restrictions: No formulas presented as rules to memorise — derive by counting.

topics.title: Compound shapes from rectangles
topics.summary: Draw compound shapes, split them into rectangles and squares, and calculate their perimeter and area.

objectives.text: Draw compound shapes that can be divided into rectangles and squares. Estimate, measure and calculate their perimeter and area.

topics.scope: L-shaped and T-shaped compound shapes on grids; split two different ways and check the total area agrees. Perimeter by tracing the outside.

units.strand: Geometry and Measure — position and transformation
units.title: Position and transformation

topics.title: Coordinates and plotting shapes
topics.summary: Compare the relative position of coordinates and plot points that join into lines and shapes in the first quadrant.

objectives.text: Compare the relative position of coordinates (with or without the aid of a grid).
Use knowledge of 2D shapes and coordinates to plot points to form lines and shapes in the first quadrant (with the aid of a grid).

topics.scope: First quadrant only, x then y. Plot three or four points and join them into a triangle or rectangle; describe relative position like 'two right and one up'.

topics.title: Translating shapes on a grid
topics.summary: Slide a 2D shape without turning it and name the corresponding points before and after.

objectives.text: Translate 2D shapes, identifying the corresponding points between the original and the translated image, on square grids.

topics.scope: Translations described as 'n right/left and m up/down'; every vertex moves the same way. Match original to image points.

topics.title: Reflecting shapes in mirror lines
topics.summary: Reflect a shape in a horizontal or vertical mirror line and use the pattern to build designs on square grids.

objectives.text: Reflect 2D shapes in both horizontal and vertical mirror lines to create patterns on square grids.

topics.scope: Vertical and horizontal mirror lines between grid lines or through a line of squares; the image is the same distance behind the mirror.

topics.title: Planning a statistics investigation
topics.summary: Plan and conduct an investigation that answers related questions, choosing what categorical, discrete or continuous data to collect.

objectives.text: Plan and conduct an investigation to answer a set of related statistical questions, considering what data to collect (categorical, discrete and continuous data).

topics.scope: One classroom-scale investigation walked end to end: question, data type decision, collection plan. Distinguish categorical, discrete and continuous with examples.
restrictions: Keep data sets to at most twenty items on screen.

topics.title: Choosing how to represent data
topics.summary: Record, organise and represent data, and explain why one representation fits a situation better than another.

objectives.text: Record, organise and represent categorical, discrete and continuous data. Choose and explain which representation to use in a given situation: Venn and Carroll diagrams, tally charts and frequency tables, bar charts, waffle diagrams, frequency diagrams for continuous data, line graphs, dot plots (one dot per data point).

topics.scope: Build one bar chart and one line graph from a small data set, then discuss when each representation is the right tool. Name the alternatives as options.
restrictions: Demonstrate bar and line charts on screen; other representations are discussed not drawn.

topics.title: Mode and median
topics.summary: Find and interpret the mode and median of a data set and judge whether each suits the context.

objectives.text: Understand that the mode and median are ways to describe and summarise data sets. Find and interpret the mode and the median, and consider their appropriateness for the context.

topics.scope: Small ordered lists: mode as most frequent, median as middle value (odd count) and the two-middle average (even count). Discuss a case where the mode is misleading.
restrictions: No mean or range — they are Stage 6.

topics.title: Interpreting patterns in data
topics.summary: Read patterns within and between data sets, answer statistical questions and discuss where variation comes from.

objectives.text: Interpret data, identifying patterns, within and between data sets, to answer statistical questions. Discuss conclusions, considering the sources of variation.

topics.scope: Compare two simple bar charts, e.g. class survey results across two weeks. Draw careful conclusions and say what might have caused differences.

topics.title: The language of likelihood
topics.summary: Describe and compare the likelihood and risk of familiar events, including ones with equally likely outcomes.

objectives.text: Use the language associated with likelihood to describe and compare likelihood and risk of familiar events, including those with equally likely outcomes.

topics.scope: A likelihood scale from impossible to certain with equally likely in the middle; everyday events placed on it, then fair-spinner outcomes.
restrictions: No fractions or numbers for probability yet.

topics.title: Equally likely and more-or-less likely outcomes
topics.summary: Recognise when outcomes are equally likely and when some are more or less likely during practical activities.

objectives.text: Recognise that some outcomes are equally likely to happen and some outcomes are more (or less) likely to happen, when doing practical activities.

topics.scope: Spinners and bags of counters: equal sections versus more sections of one colour. Reason about why landing on the bigger share is more likely.

topics.title: Chance experiments and trials
topics.summary: Run chance experiments with small and large numbers of trials and describe the results in probability language.

objectives.text: Conduct chance experiments or simulations, using small and large numbers of trials, and present and describe the results using the language of probability.

topics.scope: A coin or spinner experiment: a few trials look lumpy, many trials settle toward the expected share. Show results on a bar chart.
